A study of the historical and philosophical foundations of art education.
Problems in art education from the point of view of research and critical inquiry. One additional enrollment allowed.
Examination of various art curriculum schemes K-14: philosophies, content, methods, research, and evaluation.

Course Title: Seminar in Ancient and Medieval Art and Architecture
Description: Seminar on topics from the prehistoric to late medieval periods. Students will compose papers defending a concept/hypothesis drawn from course.

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art and Architecture
Description: Summary level course to a variety of individual topics. Each separate topic is decimalized. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 306.

Various approaches to the development and conduct of appropriate, accessible, and asset-focused art experiences in school and community programs for students with disabilities, second language learners, and other underserved populations, with an emphasis on minoritized perspectives. Clinical Experiences: 10 hours. Prerequisites: Criminal Background Check required.

Students will explore a variety of approaches to drawing, collecting, arranging, cutting apart and reconnecting, weaving, and building materials to form new images and structures. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 6 credit hours.

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art
Description: Courses focusing on a specific historical or thematic topic in European art from the early fourteenth through seventeenth century. These seminars offer an opportunity to delve deeper into specific topics regarding art history and visual culture. These seminars are discussion based, have smaller class sizes, and emphasize student responsibility and scholarly results. Students will enroll in the .0x course to receive credit. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 305
Instructor-determined course topic varies each semester. Guided inquiry into topic serves individual student exploration and development. Multiple enrollments allowed.

This course provides hands-on instruction on the manipulation and utilization of natural and artificial light for fine art photographs. Students will learn basic studio lighting and large format 4x5 view cameras. Multiple enrollments to a maximum of 6 hours. Students who have earned credit in ART 333 should consult with their advisor before enrolling in this course; there are limitations on number of total credits a student can earn in both ART 333 and 419.

Graduate level course designed to independently produce complex and effective painting that relates to relevant contemporary discourse. This course is for those who are ready to work in an intensive and self-directed manner. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 6 credit hours. Lecture and lab.
Graduate level theoretical and historical premises for making work organized by color, emphasizing interaction of surface color and light.

Introduction and survey of bibliography, methods of scholarly research, and critical evaluation of research and writings in the field. Core course for M.A. in Art, Visual Arts Sequence.

Supervised work experience in local, state, national, and international businesses, agencies, institutions, and organizations. The experience is planned, administered, and supervised at the departmental level and coordinated through Professional Practice. If the site is in an educational agency or institution, the placement must be approved by the Office of Clinical Experiences and Certification Processes. Written objectives and modes of evaluation shall be approved by the faculty supervisor and department chairperson/school director prior to the beginning of the semester. Course Title: Independent Research For The Master's Thesis

While registration beyond six hours may be permitted for the convenience of the student, he or she may not count more than a total of six hours of 499 among the hours required for the master's degree. Multiple enrollments allowed up to a maximum of 6 credit hours.

Course Title: Seminar in Ancient and Medieval Art and Architecture: Pompeii
Description:
This seminar course explores Pompeii through urban design, architecture, and public and private art, while considering its wider cultural, geographical, and historical contexts.

Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART 263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Ancient and Medieval Art and Architecture: Art of Death in Ancient Italy
Description:
This seminar examines the art and architecture that monumentalized death in ancient Italy, from the Etruscan period to early Christianity in Rome.
Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART 263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art and Architecture: Women in the arts 1400-1750
Description:
This seminar examines women as makers and consumers of art during the Renaissance and Early Modern periods. Discussions will include painting, printmaking, and architecture.
Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART 263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art/Architecture: Global Exchanges in Renaissance Art
Description: This seminar course examines the movement of art and ideas between Europe and the rest of the world, with a particular focus on exchange and hybridity. Prerequisite: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art and Architecture: Renaissance and Baroque Printmaking
Description: This seminar course focuses on the rise of printed images in the Renaissance period, with a special emphasis on key artists and cities that fostered vibrant print cultures. Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art and Architecture: Dada and Its Heritage
Description: This advanced seminar course covers the history of the Dada movement (1916-1922) and its heritage to the present. Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART 263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290.

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art and Architecture: History of Collage and Montage
Description:
This seminar course focuses on the history of collage and montage (19th Century to Present) in visual media, literature, and music.
Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art and Architecture: Contemporary Art in a Globalized World
Description:
This thematic seminar course examines the expansion of the art world beyond “Euro- America” since 1980 through the lens of a variety of conceptual frameworks.
Prerequisites: One of the following: ART 240, ART 241, ART 242, ART 244, ART 263, ART 264, ART 265, ART 266, ART 267, ART 279, ART 280, ART 283, ART 281, ART 290.

The Graphic Design Internship provides a professional experiential learning environment beyond the classroom. Description: This course will guide your investigation of the city’s urban fabric, including the houses, shops, baths, and temples used by its inhabitants. We will look at Pompeii’s urban design, public and private buildings and their decoration, and at the wider cultural, geographical, and historical contexts of the art produced by and for its residents.

Course Title: Seminar in Ancient and Medieval Art & Architecture: Art of Death in Ancient Italy
Description: Course will focus on art and architecture that monumentalized death in ancient Italy. Consider the monuments in terms of their sculptural and architectural form, and explore political and ritual motivations behind their design.

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art and Architecture - Dada and Its Heritage
Description: Course covering the history of the Dada movement (1916-1922) and its heritage to the present. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 306a01

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art - History of Collage and Montage
Description: This course will explore the history of collage and montage from the late-nineteenth century to the present, tracking artistic vision, which became progressively more fractured as society became increasingly modernized. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 306a02

Course Title: Seminar in Modern and Contemporary Art & Architecture - Art in a Globalized World
Description: This course will explore the expansion of the art world beyond “Euro- America" with a lens on Identity, The Body; Time: Memory; Place; Language: Science: Spirituality. Prerequisites: No credit if earned credit in ART 306a03.

Description: Advanced seminar covering gender and identity in art and visual culture with a focus on modern and contemporary art. We will use feminist and gender theory and the idea of intersectionality (a term that considers class, gender, race and sexuality) as a lens through which to look at the work of various artists and individuals. Prerequisites: Not for Credit if earned credit in ART 311a02.

Course Title: Seminar in Visual Culture & Theory: Text and Textiles
Description: Course examining artists who make work at the intersections of text and textile focusing on modern and contemporary artists. The course will begin with a chronological overview of textile/fiber art (weaving, embroidery, knitting/crochet, samplers, quilting, etc.) and its relationship to text, and then continue thematically (for example, attending to issues of gender & identity, social justice, poetics, narrative, collage & montage, materiality & form, and the now-historical divide of craft/art) and include work by writers/artists from antiquity to the present. prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 311a03.

Course Title: Seminar in Visual Culture, History and Theory, Thinking with Images: Critical and Visual Theory
Description: This course provides a solid grounding in the modern & contemporary critical theories most relevant to the contemporary reception and interpretation of works of art. It is also designed to assist students in articulating the methodologies used to research artists and artworks across a range of cultures and historical eras. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 311a04.

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art and Arch - Women in the Arts 1400-1750
Description: This course will examine the ways in which women negotiated complex social roles and gender norms through the study of the art, architecture and visual culture of Early Modern Europe (1400-1750). Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 305a01

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance and Baroque Art -Global Encounter and Exchange in Renaissance Art
Description: Focusing on specific moments of encounter, exchange and conflict, this seminar will examine both how art responded to global movement and the role objects may have played in the negotiations between cultures. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 305a02.

Course Title: Seminar in Renaissance & Baroque Art and Architecture: History of Printed Images
Description: This seminar explores the origins and rise of printmaking as an art form during the European Renaissance and traces its development through the seventeenth century. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in ART 305a03

Description: Examines typical development and the dynamic relationships among cognition, language, and literacy from birth through adolescence, establishing a foundation for understanding later communication and learning outcomes.

Description: Provides foundation in the typical development, mastery, and aging of cognition and language, with embedded themes of adult communication analysis, executive function, metacognition, attention, memory, working memory, neurological and behavioral changes, and literacy from adolescence through adulthood.

To provide a neurological basis of communication sciences and disorders (i.e., communication, speech, swallowing, cognition, hearing, sensory integration).

Description: Comprehensive review of normal voice production and the phenomenology of stuttering, focusing on the etiologies, diagnosis, and management of voice and resonance disorders, and evaluation and treatment of stuttering in children and adults. Review of the phenomenology of stuttering pertaining to the evaluation and treatment of stuttering in children and adults. Formerly STUTTERING II.

Description: This course addresses evaluation and management of pediatric feeding/swallowing disorders, including the needs of tracheostomized/mechanically ventilated patients. Formerly EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT OF PEDIATRIC DYSPHASIA.

Course Title: Assessment and Counseling in Culturally Responsive Practice
Description: Study of assessment and counseling approaches used with individuals with communication disorders across the lifespan. Emphasizes culturally and linguistically responsive practices to support accurate diagnosis, effective intervention, and family-centered care.

A study of counseling approaches and techniques used in assessment and intervention of individuals with communication disorders and their families.

Advanced study of classical and modern psychoacoustic theory and practice. Auditory perception in both normal and disordered systems are considered.

Administration and interpretation of audiometric procedures for differential diagnosis of auditory pathology emphasizing a test battery approach.

Course Title: Seminar in SLP: Evaluation and Treatment of Tracheostomized and Ventilator Dependent Patients
Description: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the speech-language pathologists role in the management of the tracheostomized and/or ventilator dependent patient. This course will provide students with specialized knowledge and clinical foundations for working with patients who have tracheostomies and/or require mechanical ventilation.

Description: Explores the speech-language pathologist’s role in literacy development and intervention across the lifespan. Assessment and intervention strategies related to reading and writing will be discussed.

An in-depth exploration of evidence-based caregiver coaching strategies designed to support individuals with disabilities from infancy through older adulthood. Includes examination of theoretical foundations and practical approaches to partnering with caregivers in diverse contexts.

Course Title: Seminar in SLP:  Breastfeeding Management for Healthcare Professionals
Description: Describes breastfeeding management across teams of healthcare professionals, with particular emphasis on the role of speech-language pathologists.

Course Title: Seminar in SLP Autism Spectrum Disorder and Interprofessional Practice
Description: This course examines Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) through an interprofessional and neurodiversity-affirming framework. Students explore diagnostic, behavioral, developmental, and communication approaches while collaborating with professionals across disciplines. Emphasis is placed on evidence-based, family-centered, and culturally responsive practices for supporting individuals with ASD across the lifespan.

Course Title: Seminar in SLP: Sociology of Health and Medicine
Description: An examination of how social and cultural forces shape health, illness, and the healthcare system. Challenging the assumption that health is solely a biological issue, this course uses the sociological perspective to investigate how factors like social class, race, gender, and nationality affect our health and our experiences with medical care. We will survey key topics within medical sociology and apply core theoretical frameworks to make sense of contemporary health issues.

The course examines how security vulnerabilities in devices and digital systems influence individuals, public institutions, and civic environments. Emphasis is placed on understanding technological risk, personal responsibility, and the role of hardware-based cybersecurity in maintaining trust in everyday technologies and critical public systems.

Students gain hands‑on experience with simple programming and data tools to understand how AI systems support prediction and decision making. The course emphasizes: AI literacy for all students; Critical thinking about AI opportunities and risks; Hands-on exploration; and Ethical and societal implications.  No prior programming experience is required.

Introduction to DC circuit analysis and design. Topics cover basic circuit laws, resistive circuits, Kirchhoff's laws, node and mesh analysis, Thevenin and Norton theorems, operational amplifiers, capacitors, inductors, and first-order circuits transient and steady state responses.

Prerequisites: ELE 210

Prerequisites ELE 260 and ELE 265

An advanced course in the spatial dimensions of politics and political phenomena.  Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 311.
This course focuses on monitoring gradual ecosystem changes using dense time-series of satellite data. Prerequisites: GEO 305 or GEO 405 or GEO 365.

Examination of the various types of aquifers in North America including unconsolidated vs. consolidated and sedimentary rocks vs. crystalline rocks. Formerly GEO 488a02. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 318

Quantitative approaches to understand flow, sediment, and nutrient transport in watersheds examined with special emphasis on data analysis and modeling. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 319
Theoretical and applied investigation of how cities can become more environmentally, economically, and socially sustainable and just. Prerequisite: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 322.

Introduction to karst hydrogeology, with a focus on the genesis of karst systems, the transport of fluid through the systems, and the transport and fate of solutes within the systems. Formerly GEO 488a06. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 323.

Course Description: An advanced course focusing on applications of the Python computer programming language to Geographic Information Systems (GIS).

Prerequisite: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 325.

This course focuses on a critical theoretical and applied exploration of the origins of and solutions to environmental injustices. Prerequisites: Graduate Standing. Not for credit if have had GEO 326.

Using perspectives from social and cultural geography, students will examine how places are produced by hierarchical social systems (e.g., racism, patriarchy, heterosexism), with a focus on U.S. society. Students will also study how marginalized populations have been active producers of space, creating places that support their communities and challenge inequalities. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 331.

Critical examination of how socio-political and economic systems, processes, and practices are linked globally with contemporary environmental problems. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 434.
Advanced study of the mathematics of fluid flow and the formulation of groundwater systems by computer modeling. Methods of computer modeling of pumping tests and groundwater flow systems.
This class examines how economic, social, and natural systems influence the geography of cities and shape urban life for city dwellers. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 336.
Examination of processes controlling chemical composition of groundwater from a thermodynamic point of view. Display and interpretation of geochemical data, and geochemistry of contaminants.
Overview of concepts, methods, theory and debates related to contemporary climatology and anthropogenically-driven climate change. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 341.
Investigates the dynamics of the global economy as well as the processes and actors that shape its spatial organization. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 342.
The study of the geographic distributions of species and their causes. Coursework Includes creating Species Distribution Models using GIS. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 344.

Students gain first-hand experience in collecting hydrogeologic data, reducing and displaying data, making interpretations and drawing conclusions, and producing a professional report of findings. Field trip and field work required.

Examination of the occurrence and movement of groundwater. Evaluation of aquifer materials and properties through field and laboratory measurements. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 360.

Introduction to hydrology, including all components of the hydrologic cycle, field and lab measurements, data acquisition, and quantitative problem solving. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 361.
Engineering applications of geology, construction problems of geologic origin and their engineering solutions. Field trips required. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 362.

Introduction of geographic information systems applied to geology problems. Includes vector and raster analyses of geologic, environmental, and subsurface features. Lecture and lab. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 303, 363, or 403.

Course Title: Web and Mobile GIS: Principles and Technologies
Description: The course will equip geography and non-geography students alike with the principles and essential knowledge required to manage web and mobile GIS projects, teach them the latest geospatial cloud technologies for building modern web mapping services and applications, and inspire students with real-world case studies. Prerequisite: GEO 403 or GEO 463.

Course focuses on the basics of spaceborne and airborne remote sensing, data collection, processing, and analysis for applications in hydrology.  Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 365.

Nature, behavior, and origin of volcanoes. Magmatic and eruptive processes and volcano construction. Impact of volcanism on Earth's environment. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 366.

This course is intended to provide an introduction to the theory and practice of urban planning in North America. We will explore the various fields within planning, such as housing, community development, transportation, environmental planning, urban sprawl and growth management. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 370.

Course Title: Qualitative Research Design and Methods in Human Geography
Description: An advanced course on qualitative research design and methods in Human Geography. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 375.
Origin, classification, description, and interpretation of landforms. Field trips. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 380.

Development of glaciers, glacial movements, deposits, and landforms as background for discussion of present landscapes. Field trips required. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 382.

Examination and analysis of major fossil invertebrate phyla; emphasis on groups with paleoecologic and stratigraphic significance. Lecture and lab. Field trip required. BSC 196 is recommended. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in 385.

Fundamentals of how radioactive and stable isotope systems function in high-temperature and/or whole-Earth settings. Acquisition of working knowledge of how various isotopic systems are applied to discovery and analysis of Earth processes past, present, and potentially in the future. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 387.
Application of geologic principles to field mapping and interpretation in the Black Hills and Central Rocky Mountains. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in GEO 495.

Supervised work experience in local, state, national, and international businesses, agencies, institutions, and organizations. The experience is planned, administered, and supervised at the departmental level and coordinated through Professional Practice. If the site is in an educational agency or institution, the placement must be approved by the Office of Clinical Experience and Certification Processes. Written objectives and modes of evaluation shall be approved by the faculty supervisor and department chairperson/school director prior to the beginning of the semester.  A maximum of 9 hours of total credits from the course group 393/397/400/493/498 may count toward a master's degree. Within that 9 hours, 498 is further limited to 20% of the total hours required for the degree.

Description: A student electing the thesis option must take from four to six hours of 499. Multiple enrollments allowed up to a maximum of 6 credit hours.

Primary focus is to study the structure and stratigraphy of oil bearing strata. Course Title: Independent Research For The Masters Thesis Final Year
Description: For graduate students in their final semester who have completed all course work and whose culminating experience includes a thesis, a full-time academic load would consist of at least 1 hour of 499a90. Overview of German culture from the beginning to World War I as derived from selected readings and class discussions.  Prerequisite: GER 116

Course Title: Advanced Study Of The German Language
Description: The study of linguistic concepts and their advanced application through the integration of practical work to improve language skills with appropriate theoretical topics in linguistics. Prerequisite: 2 courses beyond GER 116.

Description: Development of advanced German skills in reading, writing, speaking, and listening through a study of contemporary issues of the German-speaking countries since World War I, as reflected in essays and articles. Prerequisite: GER 217 or consent of the instructor.

Course Title: History Lab: Foundations of Historical Analysis
Description: Introduction to historical thinking and the discipline of history. Must be taken by students who begin at Illinois State no later than the end of their freshmen year, internal major transfers within a semester of acceptance, and transfer students by the end of their junior year.

Course Attributes: GE14 - HUM (Humanities H), IAI - IH3/IS8 (H2 901 / S2 902 Western Civ I)
Description: Western civilization from its beginnings in the ancient Near East until the Renaissance, emphasizing cultural and political history.

Description: Western civilization from the Renaissance to the present, emphasizing cultural and political history.

Course Title: American Diversity: Contested Visions Of The U.S. Experience
Course Attributes: CRSS - CROSSLIST (1 crse offered by 2+ subjects), GE14 - UST (United States Traditions UST)

Course Title: History Of The United States To 1865
Course Attributes: GE14 - UST (United States Traditions UST), IAI - IH6 (H2 904 U.S. History/ Civiliz I)
Description: Political, economic, social, and cultural developments from the colonial period to the Civil War. May not be taken under the P/NP option.

Course Title: History Of The United States Since 1865
Course Attributes: GE14 - UST (United States Traditions UST), IAI - IH7 (H2 905 U.S. History/ Civil II)
Description: U.S. History since the Civil War, in global context. Topics include Emancipation, forms of labor, immigration, citizenship, conceptions of race/gender, Hot/Cold wars, reform/rights movements, globalization, and state power. Students use primary sources, historical scholarship. May not be taken under the P/NP option.

Introduction to methods and debates in the discipline of history. Majors should take HIS 200 prior to taking any 300-level History courses. Must be taken by students who begin at Illinois State no later than the end of their sophomore year, and by transfer students before they take HIS 300.

Course Title: Work, Money, Power: Global Histories of Capitalism
Description: An introduction to economic history of the modern world, covering the foundational concepts and categories of labor, money, property, and commodities; as well as essential sources and methodologies.
A Global Survey of the History of Science covering varied approaches to human observations of nature from the ancient period to the present.

Course Title: Power and Diversity in Modern America
Description: This course will focus on diversity in modern US history, particularly the influence of power among various social groups in the US and how markers of difference--class, ability, ethnicity, gender, race, religion, language and sexual orientation--interact in the formation, experiences, and transformations of individual actors and complex groups.
Part one of survey of religion in the context of U.S. history to 1865.
Part two of survey of religion in the context of U.S. history since 1865.
Political and cultural evolution of the Greek World from preclassical times to the Hellenistic Age.

The climax and decline of medieval civilization.

British history from the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 to the present; political, social, and cultural history are emphasized.
Examination of life in Kievan Rus and Muscovy stressing their cultural contributions to European civilization.

HIS 136.

The history of African Americans from the Reconstruction period to the present.
A survey of the history of Illinois from the time of the French explorers to the present.

Description: The role of women in the economic, social, political, and cultural history of America from the colonial period to the Civil War.  Prerequisite: 30 hours completed.

Course Title: History of Women in the United States Since 1865
Description: The role of women in the economic, social, political, and cultural history of America from 1865 to the present.  Prerequisite: 30 hours completed.
Survey of Mexican history from the mid-18th century.
Political, social, cultural, and economic survey of Sub- Sahara African Civilization from about 1000 to about 1884 (European expansion).
Political, social, cultural, and economic survey of Modern Africa from the beginnings of European expansion to the present.
A survey of the political, socioeconomic, and cultural history of the Indian subcontinent from the 18th century to the present.
Political, social, and economic-survey of the Middle East from the 19th century to the present, emphasizing the rise of the modern nation-states.
Topical and chronological examination of Japanese religions, philosophies, art, music, literature, societal values and behavior to 1800.
Topical and chronological examination of Chinese religions, art, music, literature, societal values and behavior to 1911.
U.S. military history in a global context from the colonial period to the present.
General survey of World War II including military, diplomatic, and cultural concerns.
Intermediate study of the social, political, intellectual, and economic history of colonial Latin America (Latin America to 1821).
Intermediate study of the social, political, intellectual, and economic history of Cuba, with emphasis on the modern period.
A survey of encounters of Africans, Europeans, and Native Americans from the Iberian explorations through the abolition of slavery.
A topical course in history, taken during an international study abroad experience and led by and ISU historian.

Grade of B or better in TCH 216 or concurrent registration.
Supervised examination of issues related to the Undergraduate Teaching Experience. Seminar requires time beyond the UTA work experience. Maximum of 3 hours may be applied toward graduation.

It seeks to answer, in multiple ways, the broad question: “What is a war, and who gets to decide?”
Society, culture and government under the monarchy; destruction of the old order; rise and fall of Napoleonic France.

Description: This course examines Eastern Europe under the socialist ideological, political and economic system that prevailed there from 1945 to 1989.

This class considers what life was like for British citizens and subjects as the empire transformed over the course of three centuries of connection, oppression, and anti-colonial resistance.

Course Title: Cultures of the British Empire in the Indian Ocean World
Description: The course aims to familiarize students with the global interconnectedness of British colonialism through the study of popular culture.

Within that 9 hours, 498 is further limited to 20% of the total hours required for the degree.

Course Title: Independent Research For The Master's Thesis
Description: A student electing the thesis option must take from four to six hours of 499. While registration beyond six hours may be permitted for the convenience of the student, he or she may not count more than a total of six hours of 499 among the hours required for the master's degree. Multiple enrollments allowed up to a maximum of 6 credit hours.

Analysis of theories in mathematical thinking and learning as they relate to instruction and research in mathematics education. Prerequisite: MAT 403.

Course Title: Seminar In Research And Development In Mathematics Education
Description: Analysis of research in strategies or methods for teaching mathematics and in the learning of mathematics. Analysis of curriculum projects as they relate to these research findings. Analysis of current research and consideration of the implications of this research for new curricular innovations, and for classroom teaching.
Study of the development of mathematics education curriculum since colonial times. Readings of major books, recommendations, and papers.
Designed to provide intensive work under direct supervision of faculty on a project in mathematics education.
Intensive inquiry into topics in mathematics education through research, discussion, and reports. Multiple enrollments allowed with approval of Ph.D. director.
Analysis of the research in mathematics teaching and teacher education.
Research, library search, curriculum study, and writing related to Doctor of Philosophy dissertation requirement.

Course Title: Elements Of Mathematical Reasoning: With Math Principles
Course Attributes: GE14 - MAT (Mathematics MAT), IAI - IM10 (M1 904 General Education Math)
Description: This includes the same material covered by MAT 113, but is coordinated with the corequisite course IDS 114 for additional support.  The study of elementary counting methods, basic statistics; and elementary mathematical modeling techniques, focusing on reasoning and solving real-life problems.  Department approved calculator required.  Not for credit major or minor.  May not be taken under the P/NP option. Prerequisites: Mathematics placement exam or MAT 104 or college-level math course or 60 hours earned and 2.5 GPA. MAT 113 or MAT 113a01 are equivalent; repeat policies will apply. Must be enrolled concurrently in IDS 114.

Course Title: Effective Practices for Teaching Undergraduate Mathematics
Description: This seminar prepares graduate students for instructional roles in undergraduate mathematics courses. Topics include active learning in mathematics classrooms, effective tutoring and supplemental instruction practices, classroom communication, grading, and feedback. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum 2 credit hours earned.

Course Title: Independent Research For The Master's Thesis Last Term
Description: For graduate students in their final semester who have completed all course work and whose culminating experience includes a thesis, a full-time academic load would consist of at least 1 hour of 499a90. The 499a90 may be desirous to students who need to maintain full-time enrollment for financial aid status. Students who desire the "1 hour equals full time" designation must be approved for that designation by their graduate coordinator.
Dissertation Final Term
Understanding how firms gain and sustain competitive advantage. Topics include analyzing markets and developing company strategy across business disciplines.
Interdisciplinary course designed to provide students with an integrative perspective of contemporary business environments and development of key professional competencies.

Course Title: Applied Tools For Business Decision Making
Description: Introduction to quantitative tools used in business decision making. Students are introduced to research design, statistics, data analytics, and data visualization.

A study of how people in organizations respond to managerial and organizational practices, using a systems orientation to analyze how environmental factors influence organizational practices and climate. Topics include reactions of people to structure and control, problems of motivation and performance, resolution of inter-departmental conflicts, adaptation to change. Formerly MQM 421.
Course focus is on strategies, concepts, and tools for management of quality and the core function of producing goods and services. Formerly MQM 427.

Marketing principles, behavioral concepts, and quantitative techniques utilized in analyzing marketing problems and decisions. Emphasis on strategic and quantitative aspects of decision-making processes in marketing. A strategic marketing simulation game and/or rigorous case analyses are typical.

Analysis of financial problems of business enterprises and the formulation of financial policies. Financing of current operations and long-term capital needs, income management and expansion policies. Includes case studies. Formerly FIL 440.
Designed for non-accounting majors. Emphasis on the interpretation and use of accounting data.

An integrating course analyzing the firm in its environment with emphasis on formulation of policies and strategies and application of concepts through case studies and/or simulation exercises integrating all functional areas. Formerly MQM 485. Prerequisites: MBA 427 or concurrent registration; MBA 421, 430, and 440

Course Title: Professional Practice: Intern/Coop Ed in Management
Description: Practical experience by employment in a position involved with the management of business activities, including the analysis of business decision situations. A maximum of 3 hours may count toward the MBA degree. Prerequisites: Cumulative GPA of 3.0.

Coverage of computer-aided design concepts and an introduction to design, fabrication, and testing of operating mechanical systems. Familiarity and shop-based exposure to additive and reductive fabrication and prototyping processes. Topics include sketching, solid modeling, assembly, simulation, creation of engineering drawings, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, realization and demonstration of an original prototype mechanical device.

An introduction to the principles of static equilibrium based upon the concepts of Newtonian mechanics applied to engineered structures and mechanisms. Topics include 2D and 3D equilibrium of particles, rigid bodies and structures; reduction of force systems; vector methods; moments of inertia; friction; and analysis of structures. Prerequisites: PHY 110

This course covers the essential skills to create technical documents such as reports, design specifications, project proposals, and user manuals, as well as deliver impactful presentations tailored to diverse audiences. Emphasis is placed on clarity, precision, and audience awareness for structuring documents, using visual aids in professional communication, and adhering to industry standards.
Prerequisites: ENG 101, COM 110

This course covers mechanical engineering standards, codes, and ethics, focusing on those developed by ASME, ISO, ASTM, and ANSI. Students will explore key standards for safety, reliability, and efficiency in engineering practices. Emerging ethical challenges will be discussed through case studies illustrating the intersection of standards, codes, and ethics.

Course Title: Professional Practice: Internship In Mechanical Engineering
Description: Exploration of entry-level career opportunities. Development of professional skills and competencies of practicing engineers. CR/NC only. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum 3 hours may be applied toward graduation. Approved application required.

Analysis of deformable bodies subjected to loading including strength and deformation  analyses. Topics include axial deformation (tension and compression), Hooke’s Law, torsion, bending, shear, combined loading, stress and strain transformations, and the design of shaft, beams, columns, and pressure vessels. Prerequisites: MEC 150

This course bridges the gap between theoretical concepts of solid mechanics and their practical implementation. Students will conduct experiments to analyze material behavior using universal testing machines, strain gauges, data acquisition systems, and computational tools; and gain practical skills in materials testing, data analysis, and application of solid mechanics principles.
Prerequisites: MEC 210 or concurrent registration

This course covers the relationship between the structure, properties, processing, and performance of materials. Metals and their alloys are covered in detail; ceramics, polymers and composites are introduced in the course. Key topics include mechanical properties, thermodynamics, phase diagrams, material defects, and the structure-property relationships that govern material behavior. 
 Prerequisites: CHE 140

Use of computers (including CAD/CAM software and programmable hardware) to improve productivity and reduce cost in manufacturing. Manufacturing automation: sensors, actuators, and computers for automation, principles of computer control, and programmable logic controllers.

Introduction to thermodynamic principles, including properties of pure substances, work, heat, the first and second laws, entropy, irreversibility, exergy, vapor, power, and refrigeration cycles. Covers analysis of energy systems and thermodynamic relations, providing a foundation for fluid mechanics and heat transfer courses.

Introduction to the principles and applications of fluid statics, fluid dynamics, conservation laws (mass, momentum, and energy), similitude, and Navier-Stokes equations. Covers practical applications including viscous and inviscid flows, laminar and turbulent flows, pipe flow, boundary layers, and flow measurement techniques.  Prerequisites: MEC 230 or concurrent registration.

This course bridges the gap between theoretical concepts of fluid mechanics and their practical implementation. Students will conduct experiments that validate theoretical models of fluid statics, fluid dynamics, Bernoulli’s theorem, losses in pipes, and hydrostatic pressure. They will gain proficiency in using flow meters, manometers, hydraulic benches, and visualization tools.
Prerequisites: MEC 240 or concurrent registration

Coverage of the kinematics and dynamics of particles, rigid bodies, and mechanisms. Topics covered include force-momentum formulation, linear and angular equations of motion, energy methods, momentum methods, and an introduction to vibrations of undamped and damped systems. Prerequisites: MAT 149, MEC 150

This course introduces the fundamentals of kinematics for robot mechanisms and geometry. Students will apply knowledge of statics and dynamics to analyze the forward and reverse kinematics of spatial serial robot manipulators. Students will additionally explore manipulator-mechanism design.  Prerequisites: MEC 250.

Course Title: Numerical and Statistical Methods for Mechanical Engineers
Description:
This course introduces numerical and statistical methods for mechanical engineering problems. Students will explore key numerical techniques such as solving algebraic and differential equations, interpolation, curve fitting, and optimization, as well as statistical methods including probability, regression analysis, hypothesis testing, and design of experiments. MATLAB is used throughout the course.
Prerequisites: MAT 149

This course introduces the principles of engineering economics and project management, covering topics such as cost analysis, time value of money, net present value, rate of return, and benefit-cost analysis. Emphasis is placed on integrating economic analysis with project management methodologies for resource allocation, risk assessment, quality assurance, and sustainability.

Intensive work in a special area of the student's and faculty's interest. Each individual project is to culminate in a comprehensive written report or examination. Open only to students who are not on academic probation and who have demonstrated an ability to profit from independent study. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 3 hours may be applied toward graduation.

Course Title: Professional Practice: Internship In Mechanical Engineering
Description: Planned, supervised, paid or unpaid professional practice in a public or private organization. CR/NC only. Multiple enrollments allowed, maximum of 3 credit hours may be applied toward graduation. Approved application required.

An Honors student investigates a topic of interest within their discipline under the guidance guided by the expertise of a faculty member. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 3 hours may be applied toward graduation.

This course delves into the principles of material selection and design of machine elements. The curriculum integrates principles of design engineering with computer-aided design (CAD) software and simulation tools for virtual prototyping and performance analysis. Students will gain hands-on experience in designing mechanical systems that are safe, functional, and manufacturable.
Prerequisites: MEC 210, MEC 220

Finite element modeling, simulation, computer solutions of stress and deformation analysis, heat transfer, dynamics and vibrations.  Development of in-house code using MATLAB or Python and use and understanding of limitations of commercial finite element software packages.  Prerequisites: MEC 210, 240

Human biomechanics from macroscopic to microscopic levels. Engineering mechanics of soft tissue and hard tissue in response to static and dynamic loading. Introduction to biofluid mechanics. Review of biomaterials – applications, compositions, and mechanical properties, e.g., metals, polymers, and ceramics.  Prerequisites: MEC 210. MEC 240

This course covers the principles and applications of conduction, convection, and radiation. Emphasis is on the fundamental physics and underlying mathematics of thermal analysis for steady-steady and transient problems. By the end of the course, students have the knowledge and skills to design and analyze efficient thermal systems.
Prerequisites: MEC 240

This course bridges the gap between theoretical concepts of heat transfer and their practical implementation. Students will conduct experiments to explore conduction, convection, and radiation using traditional and modern laboratory equipment. Students will develop the skills to design, conduct, and analyze experiments in thermal systems, HVAC, and energy engineering.
Prerequisites: MEC 330 or concurrent registration

Course Title: Energy Engineering and Power Generation Systems
Description: Traditional fuels and combustion, renewable energy sources for power generation, energy storage systems, advanced power cycles, power plant design and analysis. Environmental aspects of power generation including decarbonization will also be covered. Prerequisites: MEC 230, MEC 240

Introduction to combustion processes including thermochemistry, chemical kinetics, and transport in reacting flows. Topics include chain reactions, ignition and extinction, laminar premixed and diffusion flames, flame stability, pollutant formation, and applications to internal combustion engines.  Prerequisites: MEC 330

Control of transient responses of engineering systems including stability considerations and characteristics of different control strategies. Implementation of control system analysis, signal definition and design through in-class projects.

Course Title: Control of Mechanical Engineering Systems Laboratory
Description:
This course bridges the gap between theoretical concepts of control systems and their practical implementation. Students will design, implement, analyze, and optimize control systems for various mechanical engineering applications. Key topics include feedback and feedforward control, stability analysis, dynamic system modeling, and the use of sensors, actuators, and controllers.
Prerequisites: MEC 350 or concurrent registration

Vibration analysis of discrete mechanical and continuous structures such as beams and plates. Concepts of resonance, anti-resonance, damping, and modal coupling. Modal analysis, stability, and active and passive control of vibrations. Prerequisites: MEC 350

Application of statics and dynamics to the study of mechanism kinematics including cams, linkages, and gear trains through theory, laboratory work and a project. Interfacing electrical prime movers, sensors and mechanical systems, with an emphasis on robotic systems. Analysis and design of mechanical energy transfer systems using mathematical models implemented in MATLAB and Python.
Prerequisites: MEC 350

This course is the first part of a two-semester senior project sequence. It emphasizes the early stages of the engineering design process, including problem definition, research, conceptualization, and preliminary design. Students work in teams on industry-sponsored or faculty-led projects, focusing on project planning, feasibility studies, and communication.
Prerequisites: MEC 310, MEC 330, MEC 350

This course is the second half of a senior-year sequence where students refine designs, fabricate prototypes, conduct testing, and analyze results to meet engineering specifications and industry standards. Emphasizing sustainability, safety, and compliance, students will develop comprehensive solutions, present findings, and gain practical skills for professional engineering roles.
Prerequisites: MEC 380

Planned, supervised, paid or unpaid professional practice in a public or private organization, with more comprehensive project details and responsibilities. CR/NC only. Multiple enrollments allowed, maximum of 3 credit hours may be applied toward graduation. Approved application required.

Course Attributes: BSMT - BS-SMT (BS-SMT Degree Requirement), GE14 - QR (Quantitative Reasoning QR), IAI - IM8 (M1 902 General Education Stats), MIAI - BUS901-IAI (BUS901-IAI Business Statistics)
Description: Application of statistical concepts to decision problems confronting organizations and individuals. Includes descriptive tools, probability concepts, sampling processes, statistical inference, regression, and nonparametric procedures. Includes computer applications. Formerly MQM 100. Prerequisites: MAT 120, 121, 144 or 145. Not for credit if earned credit in ECO 138.

Course Title: Diversity, Inclusion and Equity in the Workplace
Course Attributes: IDEA - IDEAS (IDEAS Graduation Requirement), GE14 - SS (Social Sciences SS)
Description: This course explores the influence of equity, diversity, inclusion, access, and belonging (EDIAB+) within the context of work. It analyzes stereotypes, prejudices, hidden biases, barriers, systemic and institutional discrimination etc. that impact workplace behavior, individual, group, and organizational level outcomes. Formerly MQM 120.
Examines the principles and practices used to measure, analyze, and represent social, scientific, technological phenomena as it relates to entrepreneurship. Formerly MQM 128.

This course develops: an understanding of the job search process; skills needed to achieve a successful search; and professionalism related to early career issues.  Formerly MQM 200. Prerequisites: Not for credit if earned credit in MGT 289a02.
Organization theories and the role of managers as leaders. Planning and control systems, decision-making, and human considerations.

Organization analysis focusing on motivation, perception, communication, coordination, and change. Administrative problems examined by theories of individual and group behavior. Formerly MQM 221.  Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MGT 220. Not for credit if earned credit in PSY 376.

A study of small businesses and owner management. Includes basic knowledge necessary to successfully start up, run, and grow a small business. Formerly MQM 223.  Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MGT 220.

A study of new venture creation. This course teaches idea generation, idea analysis, breakeven analysis, and business planning (including development of a feasibility study). Formerly MQM 224. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MGT 220.
A study in entrepreneurship in established companies through new business generation and acquisition. Formerly MQM 226. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MGT 220.

Issues related to managing the processes by which organizations transform resources into quality goods and services. Topics include operations strategy, project management, quality management, and inventory management. Formerly MQM 227.  Prerequisites: IT 150 or BIS 167 or equivalent. ACC 132; ECO 105 (or ECO 101 and 102); MAT 120 or MAT 121 or MAT 145; MGT 100 (or ECO 138 or POL 138 or PSY 138).

Intensive work in a special area of the student's interest. Each individual project is to culminate in a comprehensive written report or examination. Open only to students who are not on academic probation and who have demonstrated an ability to profit from independent study. Maximum of 6 hours may be applied toward graduation. Formerly MQM 287.

Supervised examination of issues related to the Undergraduate Teaching Experience. Seminar requires time beyond the UTA work experience. Maximum of 3 hours may be applied toward graduation. Formerly MQM 291. FIL 291 and MGT 291 are equivalent; Repeat policy will apply.

An Honors student investigates a topic of interest within their discipline under the guidance of a faculty member. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 6 hours may be applied toward graduation. Limit of 9 hours HON 299 and 395 may be combined to count toward graduation. Formerly MQM 299.

Principles and procedures relating to human resources management, including staffing, appraisal, training, compensation, and other programs for business and other organizations. Formerly MQM 323. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MGT 220.

Managing employment relations and work conditions. Emphasis on negotiating, administering labor agreements, and impact of collective bargaining on managerial practice. Formerly MQM 324. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MGT 220.

This course explores philosophical approaches to the promise and challenges of democracy. Topics covered may include oppression, privilege, inequality, mass incarceration, voter disenfranchisement, political communication, civic engagement, and alternative systems of government. Topics may include gender norms, rape culture, cisnormativity, heteronormativity, polyamory, monogamy, BDSM, porn, and safewords. Prerequisite: COM 110
An examination of the mind/body problem, consciousness, self-knowledge, mental content, mental causation, personal identity and agency.

Origins and development of Buddhist philosophy; East Asian transformation (including Zen).

Description: Students will bring philosophical methods to bear on race, racism, and anti-racism. The course will explore the metaphysics of race (with an eye toward race’s intersections with gender, nationality, disability, and class), the nature of racism, the political philosophy of anti-racism, and social epistemology. Prerequisites: Completion of 45 credit hours including in-progress credit hours.

Interdisciplinary examination of religion, emphasizing the character and evaluation of religious world views and their connections to mythologies, ethics, and ethos.

Interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of moral and social issues in relation to the cultural contexts in which they arise.

Discussion of traditional and contemporary issues, e.g., human rights, theories of justice, Marxism, civil disobedience, punishment, and the end and limit of government. Grade of C or better in 1 PHI course or 2.50 overall GPA recommended.

We will assess theories of normative jurisprudence and the rule of law alongside critical theories that conceptualize legal rhetoric and institutions – from the police, to prosecutors, to prisons – as tools for the unjust consolidation of power.

The course explores radiation from charges and dipoles, optical scattering from small particles, and the physics of nanophotonic systems.

Description: School social work practice skill development, informed by organizational theory and school policy, with emphasis on student assessment, intervention and evaluation that supports school success for all children, including historically oppressed, vulnerable and special populations.. Substance abuse research and policy, and the implications and options for prevention and treatment. Etiology, assessment, social consequences, and intervention.

Supervised practice experience in approved agencies for generalist and specialist practica. Note: SWK 498a01, 498a03, and 498a04 offered on credit/no credit basis only; no more than 4 hrs. of 498a01, or 6 hrs. of 498a03 and 498a04 combined may count toward degree program.

Course Title: Introduction To Education In The United States
Description: A critical overview of early childhood through high school education in the United States and the role of teachers and curriculum in American compulsory schooling.

Reviews the many societal cultural factors that affect learning and teaching and the application of cultural understanding to curriculum development. Prerequisite: Completion of 30 hours including in progress hours.

Course Title: Introduction to Young Adolescent Development & Middle Level Schools
Description: Explores the distinctive role of young adolescent education in the public school, contrasted with elementary and senior high school education. Formerly Becoming a Middle Grades Teacher.  Prerequisite: 30 hours completed, Criminal Background Check required, Mandatory Reporter training completed.

Essential practices and issues related to elementary education teaching: licensure, sociocultural context of teaching and learning, instructional planning and assessment, classroom management theories. Students must be enrolled in TCH 204, 205 and 208 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 210 or TCH 210a01.

Candidates will gain experience in a school (education) setting and apply the concepts and theories learned to observed classroom practices. Includes completion of clinical hours 2 days a week for 8-10 weeks (110-140 hours). Students must be enrolled in TCH 204, 205 and 208 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 210 or TCH 210A01; Criminal Background Check required and Mandatory Reporter Training Completion required.

Course Title: Literacy Instruction in Culturally & Linguistically Diverse Middle Level Classroom
Description: This course prepares teacher candidates to engage in culturally responsive research-based practices to support diverse learners in middle level classrooms.  Prerequisites: 30 hours completed.

Combines the study of theory and practice in the teaching of reading and language arts in the elementary school levels. The course focuses on foundational concepts, theory, and current research that guides reading and language arts instruction. Students must enroll in TCH 204, 205 and 208 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 210 or TCH 210A01.

Course Title: Literacy II:Reading & Language Arts In The Elementary School
Description: Extends students’ knowledge of literacy and the use of appropriate assessment measures and instrument strategies. Includes completion of 25-30 clinical hours.  Prerequisites: TCH 208. Criminal Background Check required.

Physical, social, emotional, and mental development of the child from conception through adolescence; methods of studying children and their behavior. Includes completion of 9 clinical experience hours. TCH 210 and TCH 210a01 are equivalent; Repeat policy will apply. Prerequisites: A minimum of 30 hours including in progress hours. Criminal Background Check required and Mandatory Reporter Training completed.

Course Title: The Teaching Profession In Secondary Schools
Description: Focuses on the social, economic, and political forces that influence the development, organization, and purposes of secondary schools. Includes completion of 20 clinical hours. Must be in a Teacher Education Sequence leading to 9-12 or K-12 endorsement (other than Special Education).  Prerequisites: A minimum of 45 credit hours including in progress hours. GPA of 2.50. COM 110 and ENG 101. Criminal Background Check required and Mandatory Reporter Training completed.

Course Title: Technology And Learning In A Digital World
Description: Essential practices and issues related to the strategic use of technology for teaching and learning in the PK-12 classroom.

Course Title: Prin & Practices For Teaching & Learning In Secondary School
Description: Fundamental knowledge regarding curricular planning and instructional principles and practices. Formerly Instructional And Evaluative Methods In Secondary Education. Includes completion of 50 clinical hours. Prerequisites: TCH 212 or THE 185 or THE 185a01 and THE 185a02 depending on major. GPA of 2.50. Criminal Background Check required and Mandatory Reporter Training completed.

Course Title: Integrating Multiple Literacies & Technology Across Secondary Curriculum
Description: Focus on materials and strategies/techniques that support literacy in all content areas, including traditional and digital literacies. Prerequisites: TCH 212 and 216; or depending on major one of the following options- KNR 158 or KNR 242; or MUS 217; or THE 185; or both THE 185a01 and THE 185a02. A major and cumulative GPA of 2.50.
Study of the assessment of the reading process.  Prerequisite: TCH 208 or 235 or 267 taken within seven years; or Education or Psychology measurement recommended.

Course Title: Content Area Language And Literacy In Elementary Classrooms
Description: Study of disciplinary literacy learning and instruction in the elementary school.  Prerequisites: 45 hours completed; TCH 208 or TCH 267 or concurrent registration.
This course explores personal writing processes and pedagogy, and literacy in the PK-12 classroom.  Prerequisite: Minimum of 45 credit hours including in progress hours.

Course Title: Pre-Kindergarten Education with an Emphasis on Family, Professional, and Community Collaboration
Description: This course addresses principles/practices of planning, teaching, and evaluating pre-kindergarten programs. This course emphasizes how early childhood curriculum is formed through influential theories, historical perspectives, and evidence-based practice. There is an emphasis on the value of play, living-learning experiences, and diverse perspectives in the early childhood curriculum models as well as how one's beliefs affect pedagogy and students. In addition, this course provides students with a family-centered framework, an understanding of collective diversity, and strategies for fostering collaborative partnerships among individuals with disabilities, families, professionals, and community stakeholders. Teaching strategies: readings, lectures, guest speakers, discussion, interviews, tests, and group activities. Prerequisites: Minimum 30 hours completed.

Course Title: Social Studies and Science Methods for Early Childhood
Description:
This course presents essential factors for effective and critical social studies and science instruction in grades Prek-2. Students will develop competencies in research-informed, developmentally appropriate, and culturally responsive social studies and science content, skills, methods, and assessment.
Prerequisites: Minimum 30 hours completed.

This course provides elementary majors with an understanding of the distinctive nature and identities of young adolescents, the structure and philosophy of the middle school, and how these distinctive attributes impact teaching and learning. Prerequisites: 30 hours completed.
Strategies for educating urban students.

Course Title: Teaching And Learning in Middle Level Education
Description: Organizational structure of American public education; provisions for young adolescent education; understanding the characteristics of the young adolescent student; the role of the teacher of young adolescents. Formerly Middle Level Education And The Young Adolescent. Students must enroll in TCH 233, 296 and 394 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 130 taken within seven years.

Course Title: Foundations And Assessment Of Reading In Middle Schools
Description: Theoretical bases for reading instruction as it relates to the teaching of reading to early adolescent learners. Field experience required. Formerly FOUNDATIONS OF READING IN MIDDLE LEVEL EDUCATION.  Prerequisites: 30 hours completed.
Focus on genres of adolescent literature to teach the literacy skills required in middle level English language arts classrooms.  Prerequisites: 30 hours completed

Course Title: English Language Arts Writing Methods For Middle School
Description: This course explores English language arts writing methods for the middle school classroom.  Prerequisites: 30 hours completed

Course Title: English Language Arts Literature Methods For Middle School
Description: Connects theoretical bases for effective teaching to practical applications in a middle level English language arts classroom. Formerly LITERATURE METHODS FOR MIDDLE SCHOOL.  Prerequisite: TCH 233 or concurrent registration.

Course Title: Teaching Scientific Inquiry to Middle Level Teachers
Description: Introduces students to scientific inquiry by examining science as a way of knowing and experiencing scientific inquiry in the middle-level classroom. Prerequisite: TCH 130 or concurrent registration.

Course Title: Social Studies Content Inquiry in the Middle School Classroom
Description: This course approaches social studies content (concepts, events, processes, etc.) as venues for scholarly inquiry. Through the disciplinary lenses of civics, economics, geography, and history, preservice teachers will integrate subject content with inquiry techniques and pedagogies from the four disciplines to create products that are appropriate for use in middle school classrooms. Emphasis will be placed on how professionals in the field use inquiry skills and how students use inquiry skills in their lives outside of schools, in local settings. Prerequisites: TCH 130 or concurrent registration.

Course Title: Inquiry in the Middle Level ELA Classroom
Description: This course aligns closely with the inquiry standard in the National Board for Professional Teaching ELA Standards by demonstrating ways to instill a sense of wonder in students and the disposition to seek out complex answers. Teacher candidates will examine the various facets of inquiry, including frameworks to guide instruction. This methods course focuses on effective instructional approaches that help early adolescents frame complex questions and develop the skills to seek out and communicate answers. Teacher candidates will also learn how to effectively integrate families and communities, as well as technology, when integrating inquiry into the ELA classroom.
Explores scientific inquiry by examining science as a way of knowing and by experiencing scientific inquiry in the elementary classroom. Prerequisite: TCH 210.

Course Title: Foundations For Effective Practice With English Learners
Description: This course introduces candidates to the cultural and linguistic diversity of elementary aged students, including English Language Learners (ELs), in classrooms, schools, and communities.  Prerequisite: TCH 130 or TCH 210 or TCH 210a01 or concurrent registration. Minimum of 30 credit hours including in progress hours

Course Title: Literacy, Technology, and Pedagogical Practices in Secondary Schools
Description: This six-credit hour course focuses on fundamental knowledge regarding curricular planning and instructional practices at the secondary level, with a special emphasis on strategies/techniques and resources that support traditional and digital literacies across all content areas. Includes completion of 50 clinical hours in TCH 216aXX (lab). TCH 212 or THE 185 or THE 185a01 and THE 185a02 depending on major. GPA of 2.50. Criminal Background Check required and Mandatory Reporter Training completed

Methods associated with effective grades 1-6 science instruction. Emphasis placed upon activity-based instructional strategies. TCH 208 and 209 taken within seven years. Students must be enrolled in TCH 257, 258, 260, and 264 in the same semester. TCH 247, TCH 208 and 209 taken within seven years. Prerequisites: TCH 208, TCH 209 and TCH 247

Methods essential to effective grades 1-6 social studies instruction. Focuses on current directions, research, and individual needs of diverse student populations. Elementary classroom clinical experience providing an understanding of the strengths and needs of diverse learners in grades 1 through 6.  Includes completion of clinical hours 2 days per week for 12-14 weeks of the semester (approximately 144 hours). Students must be registered for TCH 257, 258, and 264 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 208 and 209 taken within seven years. Criminal Background Check required.
Study of the reading process with digital texts and in digital environments.

The curriculum organization, instructional strategies, and instructional materials for literacy programs. Includes satisfactory completion Clinical Experiences. Students must be enrolled in TCH 257, 258, 260, and 264 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 208 and 209 or 235 or 267. A minimum of 75 hours completed.

Course Title: Curriculum And Pedagogical Issues In A Global Society
Description: An introduction to educational systems and institutions in a non-U.S. context.   Admission to a teacher education program and concurrent participation in a study abroad program required.

Course Title: Language Arts In The Early Childhood Classroom
Description: This course provides instruction across dimensions of primary language arts, focused on research-informed practices differentiated to meet identified learner needs. Completion of a TB test required. Students must enroll in TCH 267, 276, 293 and 314 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 271  and TCH 273

Content, methods and materials for teaching math to children at the pre-kindergarten through second grade level. Students must enroll in TCH 268, 271, 273 and 292 in the same semester. Prerequisites: C or better in TCH 210 or TCH 210A01. Completion of a TB test is required.

An emphasis on planning, teaching, and evaluating programs with a focus on play, learning, materials, assessment, and working with birth - 5 year families. Students must enroll in TCH 268, 271, 273 and 292 in the same semester. Prerequisites: grade of C or better in TCH 210 or TCH 210A01. Completion of a TB test is required.

Promotes understanding of reflective teaching and learning practices in the language arts in the early childhood classroom. Students must enroll in TCH 268, 271, 273 and 292 in the same semester. Prerequisite: TCH 210 or TCH 210a01. Completion of a TB test is required.

Extension of knowledge of early literacy and the use of appropriate assessment measures and instructional strategies for all children in grades K-3. Students must enroll in TCH 274, 275, 277 and 294 in the same semester. Completed DCFS Health Form. Prerequisites: TCH 267

Content, methods, and materials focusing on fractions, measurement and geometry concepts for teaching at the pre-kindergarten through second grade level. Completion of DCFS Health Form required. Students must enroll in TCH 274, 275, 277 and 294 in the same semester. Prerequisite: TCH 268 and 293 taken within seven years. Completion of TB Test required.

Content about how early childhood students acquire and apply fundamental science concepts, skills, and attitudes. Students must enroll in TCH 267, 276, 293 and 314 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 271 taken within seven years. Completion of a TB test required.

Content emphasis placed on cultural universals found in geography, history, economics, and citizenship. Students must enroll in TCH 274, 275, 277 and 294 in the same semester. Completion of DCFS Health Form required.  Prerequisites: TCH 293 taken within seven years. Completion of TB Test required.

Course Title: Practices & Issues In Early Childhood Education
Description: Current and foundational issues and practices in early childhood education examined through the lens of practical experiences in student teaching.  Prerequisites: Concurrent registration in STT 399A54.

Students must enroll in TCH 233, 296 and 394 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 130 taken within seven years. Criminal Background Check required.

An Honors student investigates a topic of interest within their discipline under the guidance of a faculty member. Multiple enrollments allowed; maximum of 6 hours may be applied toward graduation. Limit of 9 hours HON 299 and 395 may be combined to count toward graduation.

This course provides future secondary educators with an understanding of appropriate teaching methods, strategies, and content for young adolescents.

Description: Survey of methods and development of materials for teaching bilingual/bicultural and English language learners. Formerly BILINGUAL/BICULTURAL METHODS AND MATERIALS.  Prerequisite: Teacher Education program; TCH 248 or 319 or concurrent registration.

Description: Methods of middle level social studies instruction for pre-service teachers. Includes examination and employment of instructional activities and curriculum materials. Prerequisites: TCH 228 or concurrent registration.

Course Title: English Learners in the Middle Level Classroom

Course Title: Special Education in Middle Level Schools
Course Attributes: CRSS - CROSSLIST (1 crse offered by 2+ subjects)

Formerly Teaching Young Adolescents With Disabilities. Equivalent course, offered as SED and TCH 394; repeat policy will apply. Students must enroll in TCH 233, 296 and 394 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 130 taken within seven years.

Course Title: Issues And Strategies In Middle Level Teaching
Description: Philosophy, functions, curricula of young adolescent education as implemented in middle schools. Relationships between pupils’ developmental characteristics, needs, and behaviors and development of school programs. Problems, issues, evaluation and accreditation of junior high/middle schools. Formerly Current Topics And Issues In Middle Level Education. Students must enroll in TCH 306, 333, 395 and 396 in the same semester. Prerequisites: TCH 233 taken within seven years.

Assignments are made on the basis of the student's area of specialization. Multiple enrollments allowed. Prerequisites: TCH 274, 275, 277, 294. Other requirements as stated in the University-Wide Teacher Education section of the catalog.

Each individual investigation is to culminate in a comprehensive written report and/or examination. Open only to graduate students who have completed considerable work in a degree program, who are in good academic standing and who have demonstrated ability to profit from independent study. A maximum of 9 hours total credits from the course group 393/397/400/493/498 may count toward a master's degree. Within that 9 hours, no more than 6 may come from 400.

Applications of technology for learning and instruction with an emphasis on critical and creative connection, creation, communication, curation, and collaboration. Evaluating technology integration to facilitate classroom instruction.
The study of the relationship between teacher reflection, planning, decision-making, and teaching practice.

This course focuses on the physical, social, emotional, and mental development of the child from conception to adolescence. It includes methods of studying children and their behavior. Prerequisites: TCH 498a02 with concurrent enrollment.

Course Title: Educational Practices and Student Diversity in Elementary Education
Description: This course focuses on the essential practices and issues related to elementary education: licensure, sociocultural context of teaching and learning, instructional planning and assessment, and classroom management theories.  Prerequisites: TCH 498a02 with concurrent enrollment.
The study of classroom learning and assessment.

This course focuses on the study of theory and practice in the teaching of reading and language arts in the elementary school levels. Understanding integrated reading and language arts programs and exploring equity and diversity in the classroom, including but not limited to language, gender, race, religion, culture, disability, and socioeconomic backgrounds. Prerequisites: TCH 498a02 with concurrent enrollment.
Examination of the student diversities found in classrooms and the impact of diverse learners on curricular and instructional practices.
Investigation, analysis, evaluation, and application of emerging and future technologies in K-20 educational settings. Prerequisites: TCH 401
The study of curriculum models, planning, and evaluation.
Explores the roles of the school librarian in management, collaboration, instruction and collection development.
Technology skills, planning, implementation and instruction in the school library, including bibliographic systems, district technology plans, and best practices for collaboration and instruction.
